```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 3
)
```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(geomfeliscatus)
```

`geom_cat()` is a pictogram geom: it draws one cat at each `x`/`y`
position. Cats are drawn in a square viewport whose size is controlled by
the `size` aesthetic, measured in millimetres, so they keep their
proportions whatever the shape of the panel.

## A first cat

```{r first-cat, fig.alt = "A single tuxedo cat drawn at the centre of an empty panel."}
ggplot(data.frame(x = 1, y = 1), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_cat(coat = "tuxedo", size = 30) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void()
```

## The five coats

`cat_coats()` lists the coats the geom knows how to draw.

```{r coats, fig.alt = "Five cats in a row, one in each coat: black, white, tuxedo, calico and tortoise."}
cats <- data.frame(
  x = seq_along(cat_coats()),
  y = 1,
  coat = cat_coats()
)

ggplot(cats, aes(x, y, coat = coat)) +
  geom_cat(size = 22) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void()
```

`coat` is an aesthetic, so it can be mapped from a column in your data.
The values are used as-is: `"calico"` means a calico cat, not a colour
from a palette. `scale_coat_discrete()` is the identity scale behind that
behaviour, and it is also where you set a title or prettier labels.

```{r coat-scale, fig.alt = "The same five cats with uppercase coat labels in the legend, titled 'Coat'."}
ggplot(cats, aes(x, y, coat = coat)) +
  geom_cat(size = 22) +
  scale_coat_discrete(name = "Coat", labels = toupper) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void()
```

## Size, angle and expression

`size` is the height of the cat in mm. `angle` rotates the cat
counter-clockwise, and `eyes` and `whiskers` are layer parameters rather
than aesthetics.

```{r variants, fig.alt = "Five cats at different sizes and angles, all with closed eyes and no whiskers."}
ggplot(cats, aes(x, y, coat = coat)) +
  geom_cat(
    size = c(14, 18, 22, 26, 30),
    angle = c(0, 15, -20, 30, 0),
    eyes = "closed",
    whiskers = FALSE
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void()
```

## Colours

`fill` replaces the base fur colour while keeping the coat's markings, and
`colour` sets the outline. `alpha` fades the whole cat.

```{r colours, fig.alt = "Three white cats with pink, blue and green fur."}
pastels <- data.frame(
  x = 1:3,
  y = 1,
  fur = c("#f6d5e0", "#d5e8f6", "#e6f6d5")
)

ggplot(pastels, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_cat(coat = "white", fill = pastels$fur, size = 26) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void()
```

## Cats in a plot

Because a cat is just a mark, it composes with the rest of the grammar:
scales, facets, positions and themes all work as usual. Map `size` when
you want the cats themselves to carry a variable.

```{r scatter, fig.alt = "A scatterplot of ten cars where each point is a cat whose size grows with horsepower."}
cars <- transform(
  mtcars[1:10, ],
  coat = rep(cat_coats(), length.out = 10)
)

ggplot(cars, aes(wt, mpg, coat = coat, size = hp)) +
  geom_cat() +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 16) +
  theme_minimal()
```
